culture:Casa-Museu Dalí, Portlligat.name: Casa-Museu Dalí, Portlligat
culture:Casa-Museu Dalí, Portlligat.teaser: Fifty years of a painter knocking fishermen's huts together into one white maze above Portlligat bay
culture:Casa-Museu Dalí, Portlligat.story: In 1930 Dalí bought a one-room fishermen's hut at Portlligat from Lídia Noguer. Over the next fifty years he and Gala bought the cottages around it and joined them, so the house now climbs the slope in a run of small rooms, narrow stairs and odd levels. You pass the library, the studio with its easels and the light he waited for, the oval room built for Gala, and climb out to the terrace under the egg on the tower. He lived and worked here until 1982, when Gala died and he left for Púbol. Groups are small and timed, so the rooms stay quiet.
culture:Casa-Museu Dalí, Portlligat.why: Go for the studio window: the bay you see from it is the bay in half his paintings.
facts: Portlligat, a short walk north over the hill from Cadaqués

culture:Museu de Cadaqués.name: Museu de Cadaqués
culture:Museu de Cadaqués.teaser: The village's own museum, in the old town, where each show is about someone who painted this bay
culture:Museu de Cadaqués.story: Portlligat shows you one painter's house; the Museu de Cadaqués, in the middle of the old town, shows you the bay through many hands. It has no permanent collection to speak of. Instead it hangs temporary exhibitions tied to the village, several a year, often built around Dalí and around the painters and musicians of the Pichot family, and it shuts for a few days between shows while the walls change. Rooms are small and cool, which makes it a sound plan for a tramuntana afternoon when the cape is too wild to walk. Check what is hanging before you climb up.
culture:Museu de Cadaqués.why: Look for the local lenders on the labels: many works come out of Cadaqués families' own houses.

culture:The colony.name: The artists' colony
culture:The colony.teaser: A village with no easy road that drew Picasso, then Lorca, Buñuel, Magritte and the woman who left with Dalí
culture:The colony.story: Cadaqués was hard to reach, which was the point. In the summer of 1910 Picasso worked here as the guest of the Pichots, a Barcelona family of painters and musicians who summered on the bay; the painter Ramon Pichot later showed the boy Dalí what modern painting looked like. In the 1920s Dalí's family house brought Lorca. Then came the summer of 1929: Buñuel, René Magritte and Georgette, the poet Paul Éluard and his wife Gala. Gala stayed with Dalí, and the colony had its central story. Duchamp and many others followed, but those weeks of 1929 changed the place.
culture:The colony.why: Walk the waterfront knowing that most of these people swam off the same rocks you are looking at.
facts: The Museu de Cadaqués often hangs Dalí and Pichot shows; the Portlligat house has its own card
'The most beautiful place in the world' is widely quoted as Dalí's verdict on Cadaqués; we have not found where he first said it

culture:Santa Maria.name: Santa Maria
culture:Santa Maria.teaser: A whitewashed church on top of the old town, hiding an altarpiece of gilded wood 23 metres high
culture:Santa Maria.story: Climb the schist lanes, laid with stones set on edge, to the white church at the top of the village. Inside, the high altar fills the whole east end: a baroque retaule of carved and gilded wood about 23 metres high and 12 wide, rising in tiers from Passion scenes through the Virgin to her Coronation, with the Evangelists on guard. Jacint Morató drew the design; in 1723 the sculptor Pau Costa contracted the work with Joan Torras of Figueres, and Josep Serrano of Girona joined them. The gilding took decades more. In summer the music festival uses the nave.
culture:Santa Maria.why: Stand at the back of the nave first, then walk up slowly: the gold gets louder with every step.
facts: The top of the old town, Cadaqués

culture:The cemetery.name: The cemetery
culture:The cemetery.teaser: Whitewashed niches stacked on a slope behind the church, every row turned to face the water
culture:The cemetery.story: Go round the back of Santa Maria and the lane drops into the village cemetery: a small terrace of whitewashed niches and family tombs built against the hill, the names of old Cadaqués families painted and carved one above the other. Nothing here is famous, and that is the reason to come. It is quiet, it smells of cypress and dry stone, and because the dead were given the best seats, every row looks over the roofs to the open bay. After the gold of the church it is a plain, honest full stop.
culture:The cemetery.why: Come straight after the church and sit for five minutes; it is the calmest high point in the village.

culture:Far de Cap de Creus.name: Far de Cap de Creus
culture:Far de Cap de Creus.teaser: Lit since 29 July 1853 on the last wind-scoured headland of the Iberian Peninsula's eastern edge
culture:Far de Cap de Creus.story: The road east from Cadaqués runs about 8 km of bends over bare rock to the end of the cape, where the lighthouse has turned since 29 July 1853. This is the easternmost point of the Iberian Peninsula, inside the Parc Natural de Cap de Creus, and on tramuntana days the north wind leans on you hard enough to change how you walk. Below, the coves of Cala Fredosa and Cala Jugadora cut into the rock; ahead is nothing but sea. The summer car restriction is over for 2026, so in October you can drive out, but autumn gusts can make the headland dangerous.
culture:Far de Cap de Creus.why: Walk past the buildings to the last rocks and look east: there is no more Spain in front of you.
facts: The end of the Cap de Creus road, about 8 km east of Cadaqués

culture:Espai Cap de Creus.name: Espai Cap de Creus
culture:Espai Cap de Creus.teaser: The natural park's centre in the old lighthouse buildings, explaining the wind, the rock and what lives on both
culture:Espai Cap de Creus.story: In the old keepers' buildings at the lighthouse, the Parc Natural runs its information and education centre, the Espai Cap de Creus. Its rooms take the cape apart one layer at a time: the geology that shaped the headland, the weather that keeps reshaping it, the people who farmed and fished here, and the plants and animals that survive the salt and the north wind, all told in photographs and graphic panels. It is small and quick to visit. Go before you walk the cape tracks, so you can read the coves and terraces as you pass them.
culture:Espai Cap de Creus.why: Ask the staff which path suits the day's wind; they know which side of the cape is sheltered.
facts: The lighthouse buildings at Cap de Creus, Cadaqués

craft:Do this one.name: Annick Galimont, La Bisbal d'Empordà
craft:Do this one.teaser: Make your own piece of ceramics in La Bisbal, the Empordà's pottery town, with the potter at your elbow
craft:Do this one.story: La Bisbal d'Empordà has lived on clay for centuries; its Terracotta museum keeps the old works, and the street of l'Aigüeta is still lined with ceramics shops. Halfway along it, the ceramist Annick Galimont has for years opened her small workshop to visitors who want to make something rather than buy it. Groups are kept to between two and five, she teaches in Catalan, Spanish, English and French, and you leave with a piece of your own. Her own work is quiet and pastel. Of everything we checked around Cadaqués, this is the craft where a named maker will actually teach you.

craft:Other two.name: The dry-stone terraces of Cap de Creus
craft:Other two.teaser: Whole hillsides of dry-stone terraces built for vines and olives, and a UNESCO craft no one teaches on the cape
craft:Other two.story: Look up from almost any cove on the cape and you will see them: dry-stone walls stepping up the slopes, built without mortar for vines and olive trees that were abandoned long ago. The circular walk to the Muntanya Negra from Cadaqués runs through these terraces, and in places the vines and olives are being brought back. The art of dry-stone walling was inscribed by UNESCO in 2018. Courses exist in Catalonia, such as Mas Bové's terrace rebuilding course in May 2026, but they are far to the south. craft:What is sold as local craft.name: What is sold as local craft
craft:What is sold as local craft.teaser: A melting clock on a magnet is merchandise, not craft: the label, not the shop window, says where it was made
craft:What is sold as local craft.story: The lanes behind the front are full of Dalí: moustache mugs, melting-clock magnets, posters of the elephants. They are souvenirs of a painter, not things made in Cadaqués, and most shops make no claim otherwise. The same goes for glazed bowls sold as Catalan or Mediterranean ceramics: some come from Empordà workshops, many give no place of making at all. We found no published case naming a Cadaqués shop, so this is a habit, not an accusation. Turn the piece over. A maker's mark and a town are good signs; a sticker with only a country is not.
craft:What is sold as local craft.why: Buy clay from the person who fired it: La Bisbal is close enough to drive to.

linger:Es Cucurucú.teaser: A lone rocky islet at the mouth of the bay, the shape every Cadaqués view seems to arrange itself around
linger:Es Cucurucú.story: Es Cucurucú, also written Cucurucuc, is a small rocky islet at the entrance to the bay, south of Punta Oliguera. It is not a café or a viewpoint you pay for: it is the thing you look at. From the terrace beside Santa Maria it sits framed between the roofs and the open sea; from the Passeig it marks where the bay ends. Kayakers paddle out to it from El Ros beach, and it is often said to turn up in Dalí's pictures. Take a coffee up from the front and give it ten minutes.

listening:No hi-fi bar, and the Boia gon.name: No hi-fi bar, and the Boia gone
listening:No hi-fi bar, and the Boia gon.teaser: No vinyl or listening bar found on this coast, and the old Boia on the beach shut in January 2025
listening:No hi-fi bar, and the Boia gon.story: We looked for a hi-fi or vinyl listening bar in Cadaqués, Roses and Figueres and found none. The room that came closest in spirit was the Boia, on Platja Gran since 1946, where Dalí, Duchamp and Josep Pla drank. It closed on 4 January 2025 after almost 80 years, under the coastal law's rule of 150 metres between beach bars, with its neighbour the Marítim about 17 metres away. Some 26 people lost their jobs and the owners appealed. In 2026 its balcony was still standing, pending a decision on its local heritage protection.
listening:No hi-fi bar, and the Boia gon.why: Walk past the empty Boia terrace on the beach and you will understand why the village mourned it.

listening:The music festival.name: Festival de Música de Cadaqués
listening:The music festival.teaser: Since 1970, summer evenings of choirs and orchestras in the village church, under the gilded altar
listening:The music festival.story: The Festival Internacional de Música de Cadaqués began in 1970, one of the oldest summer festivals on the Costa Brava, and in 1988 it gave birth to its own Orquestra de Cadaqués. Its home is the nave of Santa Maria. The 53rd edition ran from 28 June to 21 August 2026, most nights at 19:00: a staged Messiah with BCN City Ballet and the Orquestra Filharmònica del Mediterrani opened it, and the Orfeó Gracienc sang Brahms's German Requiem on 24 July. Hearing a choir fill that church, with the gold behind it, is the one concert only this village can give you.
listening:The music festival.why: Book a church concert for next summer and arrive early for a seat with a view of the altar.

listening:Havaneres.name: Havaneres
listening:Havaneres.teaser: Songs in a Cuban rhythm brought home by Catalan sailors, sung in chorus on summer nights by the sea
listening:Havaneres.story: Havaneres came back across the Atlantic with nineteenth-century Catalan sailors who traded with Cuba: slow, swaying songs in the rhythm of the habanera, about ports, girls and the sea. On this coast they are sung in groups, the audience joining the choruses, while a bowl of cremat burns in the dark. The great night is the Cantada d'Havaneres at Calella de Palafrugell on the first Saturday of July, where groups such as Port Bo have sung for decades. In Cadaqués you meet the songs in summer, on terraces and at festes; the cremat has its own card.
listening:Havaneres.why: Learn the chorus of 'La bella Lola' before you go, and you will be singing by the second round.

listening:Cap Roig.teaser: Arena names on an open-air stage in the Cap Roig gardens, about 79 km down the coast
listening:Cap Roig.story: When Cadaqués stays small and acoustic, Cap Roig is where the big names play. The festival stage stands in the clifftop botanical gardens of Cap Roig at Calella de Palafrugell, about 79 km and a little over an hour by road. The 2026 edition ran from 3 July to 18 August: Bryan Adams opened it, Miguel Ríos closed it, and Diana Krall, Rick Astley, Mika and Anastacia played in between, alongside Catalan and Spanish acts such as Amaia and Luz Casal. Going by tender or car, plan the drive home: concerts end late on a winding road.
